questions.question: When did the EU AI Act's high-risk system requirements begin enforcement?
options: August 1, 2024
February 2, 2025
August 2, 2026
August 2027
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act was in force August 1, 2024. Prohibited AI practices enforced February 2, 2025. High-risk system obligations (conformity assessment, documentation, logging) enforced August 2, 2026. Products under harmonized legislation have until August 2027.

questions.question: What are the EU AI Act fine tiers for high-risk obligation violations versus prohibited AI practices?
options: High-risk: up to €5M / 1% turnover; prohibited: up to €10M / 2% turnover
High-risk: up to €15M / 3% turnover (Art. 99(4)); prohibited: up to €35M / 7% turnover (Art. 99(3))
Both tiers: up to €20M / 4% global turnover
High-risk: up to €35M / 7% turnover; prohibited: up to €15M / 3% turnover
questions.explanation: Two-tier fine structure: Art. 99(4) covers high-risk system obligations — up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover. Art. 99(3) covers prohibited AI practices (unacceptable risk) — up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover. Applies globally if serving EU users.

questions.question: What is the defensible standard for GDPR compliance on LLM inference, and why is post-processing PII cleanup insufficient?
options: Encrypt all prompt data at rest; post-processing cleanup is equally valid
Real-time PII redaction before the LLM call; post-processing cannot undo PHI that already reached the model
Store prompts for 30 days then delete; retention limits satisfy GDPR
Obtain user consent for every prompt; post-processing cleanup is fine with consent
questions.explanation: Real-time inference-layer redaction is the defensible GDPR standard. Post-processing cleanup cannot undo PHI that already reached the model, its context window, and potentially the provider's logs. If PHI touches the model, the GDPR violation already occurred.

questions.question: What is the largest documented AI-specific GDPR fine, and who received it?
options: €50M against Meta for Facebook AI profiling
€30.5M against Clearview AI by the Dutch DPA in September 2024
€15M against OpenAI by Italy's Garante (still standing)
€100M against Google for AI training data practices
questions.explanation: The largest documented AI-specific GDPR fine is €30.5M against Clearview AI by the Dutch DPA in September 2024. Italy's Garante issued €15M against OpenAI in December 2024, but this was overturned on appeal in March 2026.

questions.question: What does cross-framework control mapping achieve?
options: Automatically generates compliance documentation for all frameworks simultaneously
Maps a single control (e.g., access control) to all relevant framework citations, reducing audit fatigue
Allows using one certification to substitute for another in enterprise deals
Synchronizes compliance deadlines across frameworks to minimize disruption
questions.explanation: Cross-framework mapping maps one control to multiple frameworks: access controls satisfy ISO 27001 A.5.15-5.18, GDPR Art. 32, and HIPAA §164.312(a) simultaneously. Implementing and auditing once covers multiple frameworks rather than three separate audits.

questions.question: When is the Colorado AI Act effective, and what does it require?
options: January 1, 2026; mandatory AI labeling for consumer products
June 30, 2026 (delayed from February 2026 by SB25B-004); impact assessments for high-risk systems and right to appeal AI decisions
August 2026; follows EU AI Act requirements exactly
Effective immediately for all Colorado-based companies
questions.explanation: Colorado AI Act effective date June 30, 2026 — delayed from February 2026 by SB25B-004. It requires impact assessments for high-risk AI systems and gives users the right to appeal AI decisions affecting them, similar to GDPR's automated decision-making provisions.
